title: Suncor v. Boulder Brings Future of State Climate Litigation Before Supreme Court - The National Law Review
content: The National Law Review uses cookies to track usage trends and patterns to better understand and improve our website. By using this website and/or clicking on any link on the website, you confirm your consent to the NLR’s placing and usage of cookies. The U.S. Supreme Court begins its new term by reviewing a closely watched climate litigation case. On October 8, the Court will hear arguments in Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County on whether communities or states may use state tort law to hold energy companies liable for alleged harms associated with global climate change. Boulder is one of roughly two dozen municipalities, along with nine states, that are seeking billions of dollars from oil companies for alleged climate-related harms. In Boulder’s case, the county filed a lawsuit in 2018 using public nuisance laws to redress in-state harms from deceptive marketing practices and upstream production activities. Boulder contends that Suncor and ExxonMobil deceived the public about the role of fossil fuels in climate change and are responsible for damages incurred by local authorities to mitigate harm to the community. Suncor and the other defendants failed to have the case removed to federal court, arguing that interstate and international greenhouse gas emissions fall under federal authority. They filed a motion to dismiss with the state district court, which was also denied. The Colorado Supreme Court reviewed the question of whether federal law preempts Boulder’s state-law claims and ruled in May 2025 that the case should proceed under Colorado law. In August 2025, Suncor and Exxon asked the Supreme Court to consider the case; their petition was granted in February 2026. The U.S. Supreme Court has outlined two questions for the litigants to address on October 8. In addition to the merits question concerning preemption, the Court has raised a threshold question of timing: whether it has statutory and Article III jurisdiction to hear the case. Boulder argues that the Supreme Court lacks jurisdiction to review the case at this stage. They contend that the companies “merely asked the state court to review the district court’s ruling and, ultimately, reverse it.” In the Brief for Respondents, Boulder states that no final judgment was entered and that the petitioners were impatient, running “to this Court at the case’s outset” rather than letting “the state judicial process play out.” Suncor and Exxon insist that the state court process has in fact played out, that the Colorado Supreme Court acted “as a court of first resort, rather than an appeals court” when it ruled the state-law tort claims were not federally preempted. If the Court accepts jurisdiction and moves to the merits of the case, the Court’s decision could have significant implications for the federal preemption question in similar climate-change lawsuits. Board of County Commissioners of Boulder County v. Suncor Energy (U.S.A.), Inc. was just the second state climate lawsuit to survive an appeal to a state’s highest court. Boulder argues its claims do not infringe on federal authority because it seeks damages for deceptive marketing practices that allegedly harmed the community, rather than the abatement or regulation of emissions. It therefore contends that the claims should proceed under state tort law rather than federal common law. In City of New York v. Chevron Corp., the Second Circuit dismissed a similar argument about the absence of a demand for regulatory relief, remarking that these climate-change lawsuits are beyond the limits of state law. The real goal of New York City’s lawsuit, according to the court, was “to effectively impose strict liability for the damages caused by fossil fuel emissions no matter where in the world those emissions were released (or who released them).” Earlier this year, the Maryland Supreme Court offered a similar warning as it dismissed three climate-change lawsuits. Justice Brynja Booth wrote: “No amount of creative pleading can masquerade the fact that the local governments are attempting to utilize state law to regulate global conduct that is purportedly causing global harm.” Lawsuits from Boulder and Honolulu have been cleared by each state’s high court to proceed to trial. Cases from New York City and three Maryland communities have been dismissed by those states’ high courts. Many expect that the Supreme Court’s decision will clarify the federal preemption question in relation to climate change litigation. The fact that almost 70 merits-stage amicus briefs were accepted by the Court illustrates the high stakes of next week’s hearing. Members of Congress take opposing positions on whether Boulder is impermissibly applying Colorado law extraterritorially. A group of 90 Democrats and Independents argue that Boulder seeks to apply Colorado tort law to obtain restitution for damages allegedly caused by the defendants’ deceptive marketing practices. They contend that the lawsuit does not seek to regulate emissions outside of the state and therefore does not intrude on federal authority. An amicus brief of 74 Republican Members of Congress states that the Colorado decision “would allow a patchwork of conflicting state laws around the country to govern matters of uniquely federal concern.” The Constitution grants Congress and the President the power to set energy policy, enact environmental standards, and direct foreign policy. Former Attorney General William Barr claims that a fundamental defect in Boulder’s case is that it intrudes on foreign policy. He warns that a “state liability regime that imposes its own costs on American companies for global emissions would necessarily alter that national balance.” Suncor claims that Boulder’s lawsuit is an attempt to set not only foreign policy but economic policy as well. Suncor and several supporting amici argue that allowing state courts to assign liability and damages for global emissions would effectively permit states to set national energy and climate policy. Boulder maintains that state courts may impose liability for local harms allegedly caused by the defendants’ conduct, even though the alleged climate-related effects involve global fossil-fuel production and emissions. A brief from the Natural Resources Defense Council supports Boulder’s position, arguing that climate attribution science has advanced to the point that scientists can quantify fossil fuel producers’ “contributions to specific extreme weather events.” A brief from climate economists disputes concerns that making energy producers pay damages would destabilize the American economy. They assert that insulating these companies from bearing the social cost of carbon is a market inefficiency that needs correction. Last year, David Bookbinder, who previously represented Boulder in the case, described the lawsuit as “a somewhat convoluted way to achieve the goals of a carbon tax,” explaining that “the people who use the products pay for the damage that they cause.” He also said that if state courts imposed liability for the costs of global climate change, the immediate result would be every fossil-fuel producer declaring bankruptcy. Courts in California, New Jersey, and Delaware have halted state climate litigation pending the Supreme Court’s decision. At present, Honolulu v. Sunoco is proceeding with discovery in Hawaii state court. Justice Samuel Alito has recused himself from the case without explanation. A 4-4 split would leave the Colorado Supreme Court’s decision in place without establishing a controlling Supreme Court precedent on the preemption question. title: Jaguars add LB and CB to Week 4 game-day roster v. Bengals - Jaguars Wire
content: The Jacksonville Jaguars are elevating two players from the practice squad to the game-day roster for the team's Week 4 matchup with the Cincinnati Bengals. Linebacker Jalen McLeod and cornerback Jabbar Muhammad will be available for Sunday's game. This will be McLeod's third and final practice squad elevation. Moving forward, if the Jaguars want him available on game days, he will have to be signed to the 53-man roster. McLeod has filled a special-teams-heavy role over the last two weeks, playing 20 combined snaps, primarily on the kick return and kick coverage units. Muhammad's elevation comes as the Jaguars are dealing with injuries at cornerback. Both Montaric Brown (hamstring) and Christian Braswell (knee) are questionable. He put together a strong showing during training camp, and the Jaguars' decision to release him during cutdowns was a bit of a surprise. If Muhammad is called upon on Sunday, he will provide depth on defense and could be tasked with filling more of a special teams role. This is Muhammad's first elevation of the 2026 season. He has two more remaining.

title: Shalini V. Rao Will Join the CRUK Scotland Institute in early 2027 as a Junior Group Leader - oncodaily.com
content: Cancer Research UK Scotland Institute shared on LinkedIn: “We are excited to share that Dr Shalini V. Rao will join the CRUK Scotland Institute in early 2027 as a Junior Group Leader. The Rao Lab will study how transcription factor networks and chromatin regulation control epithelial cell identity. Her team will focus particularly on the earliest molecular events of tumour development and how the breakdown of transcriptional programmes fuels tumour evolution and cellular plasticity. Shalini undertook her PhD at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) and subsequently joined Prof Jason Carroll’s laboratory at the Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute, University of Cambridge, for her postdoctoral training. Supported by a Pancreatic Cancer UK Early Career Fellowship, her research has uncovered transcriptional and epigenetic mechanisms that regulate pancreatic cancer cell identity, plasticity and metastatic progression. At the Institute, Shalini will bring expertise in transcription factor biology, functional genomics, proteomics, single-cell technologies and advanced in vivo models. Her laboratory will use these approaches to uncover the regulatory mechanisms driving early tumour development and identify new biomarkers and therapeutic vulnerabilities.” To which Shalini V. Rao, Senior Research Associate at University of Cambridge, added: “Excited to be joining the Cancer Research UK Scotland Institute in early 2027 and setting up the Rao Lab! I am looking forward to working alongside fantastic colleagues as we explore how transcription factor networks and chromatin regulation shape cell identity during early tumour development. More details about opportunities to join the team will follow soon-watch this space!” Other articles featuring Shalini V. Rao on OncoDaily. title: Michigan v Minnesota recap, results: Wolverines fall as offense disappears in second half - Yahoo Sports
content: The Little Brown Jug is staying in Minneapolis after Minnesota beat Michigan at home for the first time in nearly 50 years. The Golden Gophers (4-1) held the Wolverines (3-2) scoreless in the second half of a 20-14 victory Saturday. It's Minnesota's first home victory over Michigan since 1977, an 18-game streak that ended with Gophers fans storming the field. "This team's heart, their how, their spirit," Minnesota coach PJ Fleck said. "Our community and state, they never stop believing in anything. This team is resilient. There's pandemonium in Minneapolis right now." Michigan held a 14-7 lead at halftime but had the ball for only 47 seconds in the third quarter because of three consecutive turnovers, the first on a muffed punt by Andrew Marsh and then an interceptions by quarterback Bryce Underwood. Michigan started the fourth quarter on another interception by Underwood, who completed 10 of 21 passes for 101 yards and a QB rating of 69. Minnesota took the lead for good on a 3-yard TD reception by Darius Taylor from Drake Lindsey, who completed 17 of 25 passes for 136 yards. Minnesota's most recent win in the series that awards The Little Brown Jug was 12 years ago in Ann Arbor. "Besides my marriage, my kids being born, this might be the best day in my life," Fleck said.

title: Reger powers Hilton with 7 touchdowns as Lipani becomes Section V all-time wins leader - 13wham.com
content: Hilton senior running back Tyler Reger (2) scored a school record seven touchdowns for Hilton in a 56-19 win at Webster Schroeder, Friday, Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Dave Yates/Pickin' Splinters) How many touchdowns did Tyler Reger score in the game? Webster, N.Y. — It was an unusual start for the undefeated Hilton Cadets on Friday night. Webster Schroeder’s Samuel Hilfiker ripped a long kick return on the first play of the game to set them up on the one before Warriors quarterback Junior Watkins made it 7-0 in 14 seconds. The ensuing kickoff, Hilton muffed the kick and barely recovered it amongst a crowd of Warrior defenders. The Cadets were trailing for the first time all season. “Wake up!” was echoed across the Hilton sideline. The senior ripped a 64-yard touchdown run on Hilton’s first play from scrimmage and added two more touchdowns in the following five minutes as the Cadets (5-0) cruised to a 56-19 win over the Warriors (2-3) at Webster Schroeder High School. “It’s definitely amazing,” Reger said about the win.”They beat us twice last year and kicked us out of the playoffs, so we knew it was going to be a big game. We came into it fired up and showed it on the field.” “It was huge,” Hilton head coach Rich Lipani said of Reger’s early score. “I thought things weren’t going to go our way tonight, but that play put us back on track.” The win gave Lipani a Section V record 231st career victory, breaking Dave Whitcomb’s record of 230. title: Who was the best player on the pitch? - England player ratings - BBC
content: Harry Kane, Anthony Gordon and Jude Bellingham all scored as England beat Croatia England produced one of their best performances in recent times as they thumped Croatia 7-0 in Rijeka. Harry Kane opened the scoring, and Jude Bellingham, Anthony Gordon and Bukayo Saka also found the net before half-time. England captain Kane then added a fifth early on in the second half before Saka scored his second from close range and substitute Morgan Rogers added a seventh to secure a dominant win. Here's how BBC Sport England reporter Alex Howell rated the players and you can see how you scored them below. Ruthless England cruise past Croatia in Nations League Bellingham unlocks new level and potential to be 'one of the greatest' Jordan Pickford: A really good decision and save when he raced out and won the ball at the feet of Ivan Perisic early on. Not tested but was lucky to not concede with Mateo Kovacic's incredible miss. 6 Jarell Quansah: Surprisingly chosen at right-back over Trent Alexander-Arnold but the Bayer Leverkusen defender does exactly what manager Thomas Tuchel wants. A powerful runner, a good defender and his ability on the ball is underrated - he showed it with a quality assist for Gordon. 8 Ezri Konsa: Not loads of defending for Konsa to do as England pinned Croatia back but it was a calm assured performance from the defender. 7 Marc Guehi: The centre-back had to take up some risky positions as England pressed man for man all over the pitch. 7 Lewis Hall: The Newcastle left-back looks a great addition to the England back four. Hall offers pace going forward and also underlapped, going into midfield to recieve the ball. 7 Elliot Anderson: Anderson has been excellent throughout this international break and produced another mature performance. The Manchester City midfielder is a crucial part of the midfield and set up Kane for England's fifth. 8 Alex Scott: The Bournemouth midfielder was given his first England start and put in a really confident performance. Scott always looked to get on the ball and did not just try to keep it safe as England dominated. 7 Jude Bellingham: The best player on the pitch. Bellingham produced a lovely pass to thread Kane through for the first goal, scored England's second and assisted Saka for England's fourth. A truly world-class player and his quality was too much for Croatia throughout the game. 9 Bukayo Saka: The winger scored twice and looks to be building a good partnership with Quansah on England's right-hand side. Saka could have had a hat-trick but missed a big chance in the second half. 8 Anthony Gordon: Playing with a huge amount of confidence and continues to show that he has gone to another level in recent months. Assisted Bellingham and scored for the fourth England game in a row. 9 Harry Kane: Just an elite finisher and his goal put England firmly in control. The captain looked full of energy, pressed from the front and showed his passing range as he enjoyed having Gordon and Bellingham supplying him. Scored England's fifth goal too. 9 Eberechi Eze (on 70, Gordon): Played as a number 10. 6 Morgan Rogers (on 70, Kane): Played on the left as England cruised to a win and produced a composed finish for England's seventh, rounding the keeper when played through on goal. 7 James Garner (on 70, Alex Scott): Some strong challenges and kept it simple. 6 Subs not used: Steele, Trafford, Alexander-Arnold, Branthwaite, Calvert-Lewin, Chalobah, Ngumoha. content: Will Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Keenan Allen play in the team's Week 4 matchup against the Washington Commanders? title: Honda Is Making Life Even More Difficult For The Toyota RAV4 With New CR-V Lease Deals - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update We've added a section pertaining to a Mazda deal that may outdo what Honda offers in APR deals for the CR-V. The Toyota RAV4 is the sales king of SUVs, moving nearly half a million units in 2025. However, 2026 could be the Honda CR-V's year to fight back. Honda is doing everything it can to close the gap, including offering deals to make it possible to lease a CR-V for considerably less than a RAV4. Lease and purchase deals often depend on region and dealer participation, but every zip code we punch in on Honda's website is showing us the same offer at this time. Based on this offer, you'd spend around $15,121 to drive this car for about three years (the first month's payment is included in the signing costs). That's not counting ownership costs, of course. You'd also have the option to purchase it at the end of the lease, typically for $21,401. "Qualified lessees only" means that not everyone will be driving this car off the lot at the same price. But, a great deal for people with perfect credit usually means a good deal for folks with less-than-perfect credit. Sometimes it also means a better deal than you'd expect if your credit kinda sucks. This is an attractive deal, but can it tempt you away from that RAV4 you had your eye on? Let's see Toyota's competing offer. The best deal we can find on a RAV4 at the moment is for $319 a month on a 2026 RAV4 LE. This deal is good through September and may be expired by the time you read this, and it might not be available in your area in the first place. But, it tells us what kind of offers Toyota is making at the moment. Toyota will let you buy the RAV4 at the end of the lease term for an estimated $27,130. Our calculations put three years of payments and up-front costs at $15,164. The expense margin seems bigger from month to month than it is when you add it all up at the end. You're only spending $43 more to drive the Toyota than you would be spending to drive the Honda. You get to keep the CR-V for a few extra months, but that's probably not a deciding factor in anyone's leasing choices. If you plan to buy the SUV at the end of the lease, the RAV4 would cost you $42,294 in total, while the CR-V would $36,522. That's a difference of $5,772 favoring Honda. If you were to walk into a dealership and buy an entry-level model with a single cash purchase – no financing – a RAV4 would cost you $31,900, with the CR-V costing you $31,520. If you plan to lease for three years and then buy the SUV, the RAV4 costs you thousands of dollars you didn't need to spend. Leasing-to-purchase simply makes no sense in a Toyota, given the brand's famously slow depreciation rates. After three years on the road, you're paying a near-new price for a car you've already driven 30,000 miles. Even if you can afford it, you'll feel like a chump buying your own used Toyota from yourself. The best purchase deal we can find for September on a RAV4 would have us paying 4.99% APR for 48 months on an entry-level model. This isn't far from what a well-qualified lessee could get with or without a promotional offer, with national interest rates averaging around 6.39% on new cars right now. Honda is offering the CR-V at 2.99% for up to 36 months, less than half the national average interest rate, with a 10% down payment. This deal is good until November 2, 2026. Toyota may not have a RAV4 APR offer to compete with the CR-V deal mentioned above, but another Japanese competitor might: Mazda is offering the 2026 CX-5 on 0% APR for up to 36 months, at $27.78 per month for every $1,000 finances - there is no downpayment required. This deal is also valid until November 2, 2026. If we want to pay this off as soon as possible, a three-year loan on a CR-V at 2.99%, with a $3,152 down payment and 6% sales tax, would cost us $852 a month. That comes to $1,370 in total loan interest and a purchase price of $33,834. The same deal on a RAV4, at 4.99% a month, would cost us $919 a month, for $2,415 in interest, and a total cost of $36,230. These numbers are all hypothetical. Not all buyers qualify for 2.99% APR on the Honda, and not everyone would want a three-year payment plan. But no matter how you split it, you're saving money on the CR-V over the RAV4. The amount you save could be pocket change on a lease, but it could be a year's mortgage on a purchase. We want to hear from you. When it comes to the perfect male physique, our thoughts often return to a certain Hollywood icon's V-line abs in Fight Club. There’s good reason Brad Pitt's body in that movie inspired a TikTok trend: he’s lithe yet muscular, slim but with some size. And, of course, he has the prized V-line shape to his abs. You may also remember a similar set of muscles from that era, on the singer D'Angelo in his video for “Untitled (How Does It Feel).” They're the ultimate sign of a dialed-in fitness routine. But just what are they, and how can you get them? “V lines are where the obliques meet the transversus abdominis muscles. They are only visible when you have a very low body fat percentage, which can either mean 11% or lower for men, and 14% or lower for women,” explains David Wiener, a training and nutrition specialist at the AI-based fitness coaching app Freeletics. Wiener says that V lines are “highly sought after”—and require a lot of effort and commitment to achieve. Doing 50 sit-ups three times a week will not get your there. “The best way to work towards this goal is through a calorie deficit, targeted training and the right mind-set,” Wiener explains, adding that “some people may not find this a sustainable way to live, and therefore it can make achieving and keeping V lines unattainable.” We have to stress this last part. While we all have obliques and transversus abdominis muscles, having visible V lines isn’t “normal” by any stretch of the word. Getting them requires pushing beyond your limitations and taking your workout routine to the next level. And the benefits are purely aesthetic. “Furthermore, a low body fat percentage doesn’t necessary equate to optimum health,” Wiener says. “I would advise seeking professional opinion with your regime. And, genetics can either mean it's easier to achieve, or a much harder task.” Still want to get V-‘d up? Read on for Wiener’s tips for unleashing your inner Tyler Durden. V lines are doable, as long as you’re willing to put the work in, and stick with it. “A lot of people assume reducing body fat is a really hard process, but as long as you are focusing on good nutrition while staying in a calorie deficit, and participate in a good training regime, you will see results,” says Wiener. Once you know your motivation, make sure you keep it top of mind stay as you pursue your goal week after week. “Gaining V lines doesn’t mean putting 110% into your intensity of workouts, but rather 110% into your commitment for a lifestyle change, and the amount of time and motivation you put into your regime,” Wiener says. Knowing why you’re doing it will help when your commitment wavers. It can be tempting to think that getting an extreme result requires an extreme routine. Not necessarily. “Gaining V lines can be a tough process, but you do not need to be participating in high-intensity cardio every day or lifting really heavy weights,” says Wiener. “As long as your heart rate is in the cardio zone [70-80% of your max heart rate], you can reduce body fat with low intensity cardio—although you do need to be taking part in this cardio for longer amount of time to see results. The recommended 30 minutes a day will simply not be enough to get V lines.” “Being in a calorie deficit can mean a reduction in energy, especially if you are participating in more exercise than you normally would,” says Wiener. “However, focusing on the correct foods rather than less food is the answer to you succeeding and maintaining good energy levels. Eating smaller, more frequent meals which are protein-rich and contain complex carbohydrates can help to ensure you stay in a macros and caloric deficit.” Adding five more minutes on the treadmill or a few more reps per weights round can make a difference. “Adding extra reps into your routine will definitely help encourage V lines and their muscle prominence,” says Wiener. “You need to constantly be working your muscles to encourage the blood flow to your muscles, which will result in your V lines being more prominent.” The key to staying nourished throughout a training plan is to think ahead. “With the right meals, timing and portion control, you can eat every two or three hours, stay full, and still drop fat around your abdomen,” says Wiener. “Ideal foods to include in your diet include chicken, turkey, salmon, eggs, sweet potatoes, brown rice, and non-starchy vegetables such as broccoli, cauliflower, and spinach.” The Freeletics Dione workout is excellent for enhancing cardio fitness and losing weight. It doesn’t require any equipment, just willpower. It consists of three rounds of 75 jumping jacks, 50 leg levers, 25 burpees, and 50 sit-ups. Aim to complete it in under an hour. No one really cares whether you have V lines. If you want to get in great shape, it should be for you alone. And, if you’re doing that, you have to accept that might not get them anyway. “Everybody is completely different,” says Wiener. “Due to genetics, some people simply might not be able to get really visual V lines, and some people might find it really easy to get visual V lines.” And there’s nothing wrong with that. 10 Ways to Build Muscle as Fast as Humanly Possible How to Catch Up on Sleep the Right Way, According to Experts Matt Damon Did a Gut Cleanse to Prepare for The Odyssey—Should You Try One? title: Fiery as ever, Hilton's Lipani sets Section V football wins record - Democrat and Chronicle
content: Rich Lipani spent much of the last week downplaying the significance of Section V's all-time wins record, referring to the chase as a function of his experience. That chase is now over. Hilton's longtime head coach, still fiery as ever, stands alone atop the area's record books. No. 231, a dominant 56-19 victory for the Cadets over Webster Schroeder, pushed Lipani past Dave Whitcomb, who held the record for the last couple years. "It's fantastic. A lot of the guys I've coached over the years that aren't with the team anymore were back tonight to help celebrate a little bit," Lipani said. "It's a great night overall, but we'll move on to next week and see what happens." Lipani nabbed win No. 1 some 40 years ago as head coach at Greece Arcadia. The former three-sport star at Greece Athena had recently finished his playing career at SUNY Brockport, and in 1986 took over a Titans program with little football tradition. Within two years, Arcadia won its first (and only) Section V football title. Following a three-year stint Lipani relocated slightly west to Hilton, where he was already a physical education teacher. In 1988, the year before Lipani was hired, the Cadets endured a winless season. And within a few years, again, Lipani turned that team into a championship winner. Now the four-time section title-winning head coach is to Section V what Don Shula is to professionals. Beyond the win total, Hilton assistant coach Andy Forman — who played under Lipani at Arcadia — thinks his head coach's longevity deserves recognition. A coach that sticks around for 40 years is a rare one indeed. "Nobody coaches that long anymore. He's a special guy to be able to do it. He's been able to adapt and overcome," Forman said. "His big message is that he wants football to be the best time of the kids' life when they're here at Hilton. That's what he really strives for." Forman acknowledges Lipani's sideline intensity, another trait from a bygone era, but said the coach's impassioned demeanor doesn't tell the entire story. "He's the most intense guy I've ever seen. We weren't much of a football school at Arcadia before he came, but his intensity was contagious right away. He brings it now the same way he did in '86," Forman said. "But he's one of the funniest guys you'll ever meet. You might not think that when you see him on the sidelines, but he's the best." There was little to laugh about on the opening play of Friday's game, when Schroeder's Sam Hilfiker took the opening kickoff about 70 yards to the doorstep of the end zone. Schroeder took the lead on the next play, only 13 seconds into the game. It was an unfamiliar position for the perfect Cadets, but not long-lasting. On Hilton's first offensive play from scrimmage, senior Tyler Reger dashed left for a 74-yard score. The first play of the Cadets' second possession, Reger again attacked the left sideline for an 83-yard touchdown run. By game's end, Reger had nearly upstaged his coach's historic night. His seven touchdowns were one short of the Section V record, held by a handful of ex-players. "(The opening kickoff) made us have to do something we haven't had to yet. We had to bounce back, with our backs against the wall a little bit there. That was a big drive for us after. That's what we've been preaching all year, because that's what it's gonna take down the road." Unbeaten and averaging about 48 points through five weeks, Hilton shows no signs of slowing down. Neither does its coach. Asked how long he wants to continue in his role in a recent appearance on the Varsity Voices video podcast, Lipani offered no expiration date. “If they want me back and I feel I’m doing a good job, I’ll come back for another year. If I think I’m not doing a good job, I’ll step away,” Lipani said. “Just doing the best I can every day. The guys I’ve got working with me are doing a great job and we all enjoy it. One day at a time, one year at a time.” Totals accumulated by the New York State Sportswriters Association Our editors independently choose our recommendations. title: Republic of Ireland news conference ends abruptly amid accusations - BBC
content: The Republic of Ireland's news conference before their second match against Israel ended abruptly as head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson fielded questions from Israeli journalists. One reporter tried to ask Hallgrimsson for his thoughts about the incident on Wednesday when a co-pilot attacked a pilot on a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv before passengers overpowered the attacker and successfully took control of the plane. The Republic of Ireland manager was also asked by another journalist, who refused to give up the microphone, about alleged racism by Irish players during last Sunday's 3-0 win over Israel in Hungary. The news conference was brought to a close at that point by Football Association of Ireland (FAI) communications manager Kieran Crowley, who said those allegations were "completely untrue" as the mood soured. Allegations of racism by Irish players follow on from the FAI announcing it is investigating reports of racist abuse directed towards Republic of Ireland striker Adam Idah by Israel fans during the first match in Debrecen, which Hallgrimsson's team won 3-0. At Israel's news conference later in the day, the team's media officer stepped in to confirm the Israel FA has not lodged a complaint with Uefa but "will think about that after the match tomorrow". "Our players told us there was trash talk between the Irish players and them that was not like normal or like any other match," the media officer said. Head coach Ran Ben-Shimon did not want to address such matters, insisting "a good result tomorrow is my only focus". Before the Irish news conference was cut short, Hallgrimsson said similar as he stressed he would not "get involved in that as others will process that". "It is a game with a lot of emotions attached," Hallgrimsson said. "I haven't read anything and it's not something I want to get involved with. It goes to a process, both in our department and with Uefa. "Something was reported by both teams, so I just hope we can focus on football and football will be the winner after this. "I have not gone into details looking at this as I have enough to think about." Second Israel game won't be a friendly - Hallgrimsson Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious Hallgrimsson's side face Israel in Serbia on Sunday after their 3-0 win over the same opposition last week This has been a challenging international window for the Republic of Ireland, with the Israel fixtures dominating discourse in Irish football. Since the teams were drawn together in February, a 'Stop The Game' campaign was launched by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine, which called for a boycott of the fixtures in protest against the ongoing Israel-Gaza war. Before last week's 'home' game for Israel in Hungary, Republic of Ireland goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrew from the fixtures, saying "it would be wrong to participate", while a vote by players to play the games passed by a "significant majority", according to FAI chief executive David Courell. The players wore black armbands during the game "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict". The Republic of Ireland then played Austria in Dublin on Thursday, when protests resulted in tennis balls being thrown on to the pitch and a protester briefly interrupting the game when he ran on to the turf, waving a Palestine flag. Hallgrimsson said under the circumstances, it will be a "a big win for this group and the association if we go through undamaged". They have four points from three games so far, having beaten Israel and drawn 2-2 with Austria. They lost 1-0 to Kosovo in the campaign opener. "The most pleasing thing for me is to see the togetherness and how they stand up for each other," Hallgrimsson said. "Whatever they have done, they have done it with respect to the situation, to each other and after this, this bond of brothers will be stronger than ever. All the obstacles this group will face in the future will be lesser than it is. "When we look back, this camp will be a moment we grew the most and stepped up as leaders, supported each other and stuck together. The power of togetherness is stronger than individuals." The Republic of Ireland boss revealed the team have taken part in a group prayer before leaving the dressing room for recent games, which he said was "just to cool our heads before we go on to the pitch". He said that has been led by midfielder Conor Coventry whom he joked is now known within the squad as "Brother Coventry". The Icelander said Dara O'Shea - the team's captain in place of the injured Nathan Collins - was not with the squad, as his wife was due to give birth. He may arrive back in Backa Topola prior to Sunday's 19:45 BST kick-off. title: Final Boss Battle Of The Manual Super Sedans: Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing Vs. BMW M3 CS Manual - CarBuzz
content: Subscribe to the CarBuzz newsletter to never miss an update It’s wrong to eulogize someone that’s still alive. Maybe even bad luck. But we can’t help but mourn what we know can't last forever. New gas-powered, driver-centric vehicles are disappearing from showrooms. Among them, even fewer sedans combine big power up front with power sent to the rear. Somewhere in between, there’s a gearbox installed for the sake of pure enjoyment. No two cars epitomize this trade-off to computerized perfection for simple joys more than the burly Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing and the agile BMW M3 CS Handschalter. Both of them might very well be the last of their kind. Go ahead, count how many sedans you can buy in 2026 with manual transmissions. Now, how many of those have V8s or turbocharged inline-six powerplants as beating hearts? How many of them come with a manual transmission? Forgive the cliché, but not long ago the answer would have been more than the two we can think of. That’s not to say the two we’re left with are the ones we don’t want. In fact, they’re the only two we’d rather have than anything else. Allow us to introduce them. We never doubted Cadillac could build a fire-breathing muscle car, but its first stab at it in 2004 answered a question we don’t remember asking. For $50,000, Cadillac was selling the CTS-V, bringing a swift end to the brand's reputation for building vehicles with boat-like handling. As the first fast Cadillac in years, the CTS-V had the job of establishing General Motors’ luxury marque as a formidable adversary to any German sport sedan in the new millennium. Over two decades later, that $50,000 base price for these high-performance Cadillacs has ballooned to $100,000. The 2026 CT5-V Blackwing carries the torch for the brand's flagship V-Series vehicles today, packing a fire-breathing V8, a manual gearbox, and comfy leather seats only Cadillac could produce. The 6.2-liter supercharged V8 thumps out 668 horsepower and 659 lb-ft of torque and hands the driver control of six gear ratios. At the top of the M3 range is the CS. Unlike any modern Competition Sport model, however, the 2027 M3 CS Handschalter edition replaced the eight-speed paddle-shift automatic with a proper “hand-shift” gearbox, as its German name implies. Available in limited quantities, it cost a whole Toyota Corolla more than the standard M3 and shared the same 473 horsepower output from a twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six. The CS Handschalter returned less car for more money, but that’s precisely what made it fantastic. The model came standard with the expensive carbon fiber package, which helped bring the weight below the standard M3, and used suspension pieces from the M4 CSL. Despite its high sticker price, the M3 CS Handschalter was still $10,000 cheaper than the automatic-only CS sold from 2023-2024. BMW made this version of the M3 available exclusively in North America in “very limited numbers,” thanks to high demand for a manual, lightweight sport sedan. Even with different approaches to their flagship sport sedans, the CT5-V Blackwing and M3 CS Handschalter are cut from the same cloth. They honor their heritage in separate ways, to say nothing of their being the last two clutch-kicking four-door sedans built for high-horsepower chicanery. They differ in how they honor their roots. All BMW M cars today are bigger, faster, and heavier than the ones that came before, making CS models even more important for cutting weight and restoring some semblance of authenticity. BMW’s M division used to make race-bred, uncomfortable, loud coupes and sedans so the public could get a taste of its Group A German Touring Car Championship victories. Now, they pack more luxury features than ever before, offsetting the extra weight with more horsepower. Compared to the original CTS-V, the CT5 is longer, wider, heavier, way more expensive, and a bit crude in an age of mild hybrids. But it’s faster, and that’s all it needs to make it better. The best way the CT5 honors where it came from is by keeping its V8 and packing in the horsepower like an overstuffed suitcase. This leads us to two modern interpretations of the best of each – both of which make a heartfelt attempt to convince us they pack everything we loved about their original forms. Cadillac doesn’t need to do much convincing, but BMW is trying to prove it still knows how to build a lightweight, race-bred sedan. The result, thankfully, isn’t a try-hard M3 CS. Instead, it’s the best interpretation of the M3 in its sixth generation. Both are, without a doubt, the best sports sedans in the business. Right about now we’d craft a ploy suggesting you go out and buy one of these fantastic sedans, but good luck finding one listed without horrendous dealer markups, if you can find one at all. The M3 CS Handschalter is a limited edition, with only 40 units making their way to Canada and an unspecified amount reserved for the US. In comparison, the Cadillac often comes with significant dealership markups, taking an expensive CT5-V Blackwing and making it even pricier. These two land between $110,000 and $150,000 depending on options, trims, and how benevolent (or not) a dealer is. There’s a small list of cars we’d think of in addition to these two at this price point, including but not limited to the Porsche 911 Carrera T, Chevrolet Corvette Z06, and maybe even the Mercedes-AMG GT 55 Coupe. The downside of being two of the best sports sedans is that they're also quite expensive, which opens the door to tough competition from others at the same price. If a combustion engine and four doors are all that matters to you, then there's the AMG GT 63 S E Performance four-door coupe. It packs a twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V8 with an electric motor powering the rear axle. The setup makes a total of 831 hp and comes with a nine-speed automatic gearbox. The sedan starts at a hefty $200,500. But forget the steep price tag for a moment and revel in the fact that we still have two four-door, five-seat sedans that can handle all aspects of family life and still turn competitive lap times on the weekend. We’re not declaring a winner in this round of car versus car because both won by just showing up. And they’re still here, but we don’t know for how much longer. BMW launched the next-generation 3 Series, built alongside an electric model, meaning it’s no longer optimized for one powertrain like it has been for 40 years. Cadillac promised a next-generation CT5, Blackwing included, but what does that look like as we inch closer to the decade when all Cadillacs are said to be EV-only? Does it keep its V8 but only in hybrid form? Will we still be able to change our own gears? Rather than wait in fear for what’s next, we want to enjoy what we have now before it’s gone completely. That’s not to say what comes next will be fantastic, but it’s more than clear it won’t be anything like what we have now. We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful. There is, and always will be a market for these cars. And he’s a shame they are slowly phasing them out.  GM and BMW would be wise to keep these around as they will sell every one they produce with a manual and can virtually set any price.  It won’t matter. Even the secondhand market is strong for these cars. Manuals tend to sell for a higher premium due to rarity, and they sell fast. title: CBS News poll finds voters split on state v. national focus in tied Maine Senate race - CBS News
content:
Updated on:  October 2, 2026 / 10:10 PM EDT
            / CBS News Anyone who's walked its rugged coast or skied in its mountains knows Maine can get windy.But right now Maine's Senate race seems a bit insulated from the national political winds — which otherwise seem to favor the Democrats — at least enough to keep incumbent Republican Susan Collins in a tied race with Democrat Troy Jackson in a state that otherwise has a Democratic-leaning electorate. Collins is drawing enough voters and enough of Maine's Democrats, while she is bolstered by those who say they're voting more on state matters than national ones, to keep the race at a tie. And she has an edge on who would bring back more federal funds to Maine. Jackson's challenge is that Collins peels off one in five voters who disapprove of Trump — a rate higher than what Republican congressional candidates get nationally. Jackson's backing, in turn, is driven by those who think Collins is too much in agreement with President Trump, as well as by voters specifically opposed to tariffs, by those trying to give national Democrats control of the Senate and by those prioritizing change over experience. A sizable 10% of voters say they could still change their minds — another dynamic that underscores that this could still break either way. Even when voters think Jackson's policies would make them financially better off, Collins gets almost one in five of those voters, too. Overall, Maine's voters do feel Trump's policies have hurt the Maine economy. Jackson wins most of those who do. But long-time service isn't entirely working against Collins, even if it's an "anti-incumbent" year: Collins does especially well among voters who say they've voted for her multiple times in the past. Jackson may be feeling the effects of the primary season: four in 10 Democrats and most independents wish someone else were the Democratic nominee. Jackson also runs behind the Democrats' gubernatorial nominee Hannah Pingree, as Pingree's lead in the governor's race hews much more closely to the state's overall partisan lean. (Kamala Harris won the state.) Pingree gets some of the voters who are splitting their tickets to back Collins. This CBS News/YouGov survey was conducted with a representative sample of 1,144 registered voters in Maine interviewed between September 23rd -October 1, 2026. The sample was weighted according to gender, age, race and education based on  U.S. Census data, as well as to 2024 presidential vote. The margin of error is ± 4.7 points for registered voters. title: Suncor v. Boulder: the Supreme Court climate lawsuit against Big Polluters, and what it means for you - League of Conservation Voters
content: A major fight for climate justice against Big Polluters arrives at the Supreme Court on Monday. The Court will hear arguments in Suncor v. Boulder, a climate lawsuit with high stakes for Americans’ wallets as they confront the costs of climate change. It’s no secret that fossil fuel companies knew their products would cause climate change. Taking a page from Big Tobacco’s and Big Pharma’s playbooks, they lied to the public for decades and made billions. With Suncor, the Supreme Court’s MAGA justices could help Big Polluters avoid paying for it. This case will decide whether the American people and their local and state governments can sue Big Polluters for the harms of climate change. Polluter-caused climate change costs American communities billions of dollars. Across the country, a growing number of state and local governments are filing climate lawsuits against polluting corporations to hold them responsible for their share of the cost. The story of Suncor v. Boulder starts with one such case. In 2018, officials in Boulder, Colorado sued fossil fuel companies for violations of state law. They say Boulder’s taxpayers are paying the price for Big Polluters’ greed. From wildfires to drought-induced drinking water shortages, climate change in Boulder poses many threats. Preparing for these threats and responding when they happen is costly. Boulder officials want the oil companies to pay their fair share. Now, the MAGA justices will decide whether Boulder – or anyone else in the country – can even bring this type of lawsuit. If they side with the oil companies, then ordinary Americans could be stuck paying for the entire cost of climate change (the same way we’re paying for Big Tech’s data centers!). And the MAGA justices have a long record of making it harder for regular people to hold big corporations accountable in court. As the climate changes, communities face rising risks and climbing costs. Just a few examples: In total, climate change costs American households an estimated $1,300 every year. Roughly $150 of these costs are borne by the government, which passes them on in taxes. All of this is before you count the rising costs caused by Trump canceling clean energy projects and starting a war with Iran. When disasters hit, states and localities face hundreds of millions, even billions, of dollars in damages. Meanwhile, fossil fuel companies try to avoid paying for the damage they’ve caused at every turn. Peggie Fletcher fled her flooding home in Vermont on the back of a local firefighter in July 2023. With her, she carried four shirts, a pair of pants, a toothbrush, and her medication. She was one of thousands to lose their homes after rain fell at 300 to 500 percent of normal levels in a single week. Like Boulder, Vermont sued major fossil fuel companies for violating state law. The heat dome covering the Pacific Northwest in June 2021 claimed the life of Juliana “Julie” Leon, on what was then the hottest day ever recorded in Seattle. Her air-conditioning wasn’t working as she drove home from a doctor’s appointment in 102-degree heat. She pulled over, but was unable to call for help. Julie died of hyperthermia on the side of the road. Her daughter, Misti, sued oil companies in state court for wrongful death. A local government in Oregon also sued polluters over the heat dome. A downed transmission line started a wildfire near Paradise, California in November 2018. The Camp Fire destroyed an entire town, claimed 85 lives, and burned 150,000 acres. For residents to return home, the community had to rebuild roads, schools, and the sewer system. It also had to invest heavily in wildfire prevention and detection efforts. Eight years later, the town still hasn’t fully recovered. The Camp Fire is one of many wildfires at the heart of California’s lawsuit against oil companies. When polluters may have broken the law, climate lawsuits are a critical pathway to holding them accountable. That is why eleven states, the District of Columbia, and 61 local and tribal governments have sued Big Polluters over climate change. A homeowners’ association and at least one individual have brought similar lawsuits. All rely on general liability claims under state law. They represent a tidal wave of Americans fed up with oil companies and their endless greed. This is why the fossil fuel companies are desperate to stop them. Now, these efforts to protect Americans from polluters’ greed are at risk. Polluter-backed Republicans in all three branches of the federal government are trying to shield polluters from liability. If successful, they would cut off peoples’ access to state courts as a means of holding polluters accountable. Even ordinary people like Misti Leon, who lost her mother to climate change, could be barred from suing for the loss of their loved ones, homes, and businesses. Federal courts are battling over whether oil companies can be sued for violating state law. In New York City’s case, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit ruled for the oil companies. Yet, federal district courts in other circuits have allowed lawsuits to continue. This term, the Republican-majority Supreme Court will decide the fate of these climate lawsuits and the right of other communities to bring similar lawsuits. Ruling for the fossil fuel companies would require the MAGA justices to make enormous leaps in their legal reasoning. However, several of the MAGA justices stand to benefit from doing so. Justice Samuel Alito owns holdings in oil and gas stock worth tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of dollars. The value of those stocks could fall if the court were to decide that states could sue polluters. For months, environmental and anti-corruption organizations, including the League of Conservation Voters, called for Alito to recuse himself from the case. He waited until just a week before arguments to do so. This is the second time that Alito has recused himself from a case involving an oil company he has a financial interest in at the eleventh hour. He’s proven his pro-polluter stance in other cases, including a major attack on clean water just three years ago. Most importantly, Alito’s recusal is unlikely to change the outcome of Suncor v. Boulder. The MAGA justices have the majority with or without him. And, Alito is not the only justice in that majority with ties to the oil and gas industry. Among others, Justice Clarence Thomas has joined many Supreme Court decisions in favor of fossil fuel companies. He is infamous for accepting extravagant gifts from billionaires. Among his many conflicts of interest are ties to oil company executives. Yet Thomas has not recused himself. As a result, the decision’s legitimacy is in doubt before arguments even begin. Thus, Suncor v. Boulder is likely to join the long list of the MAGA majority’s landmark anti-environment decisions. West Virginia v. EPA severely undermined EPA authority to fight climate change under the Clean Air Act. Sackett v. EPA rolled back Clean Water Act protections for millions of miles of streams and tens of millions of acres of wetlands in the United States, jeopardizing the drinking water of millions of Americans. With Suncor, the pro-polluter MAGA justices are poised to strip ordinary Americans of their access to justice in state courts and give polluters free rein to continue destroying the climate. The judiciary is not the only branch where Republicans are working to protect polluters from the people. In 2024, Trump promised oil executives favors if they contributed to his presidential campaign. Oil-and-gas industry executives, PACs, and donor-advised funds donated $201 million to Trump and GOP campaigns, including ad spending. They also donated $19 million to Trump’s inaugural fund. Then, Trump delivered on his promise. He has used the Department of Justice (DOJ) to protect polluters. In 2025, the DOJ sued Vermont and New York to stop their climate superfund laws. These laws would make polluters pay for the states’ climate adaptation and mitigation projects. In places with flooding, that could include turning parking lots into basins to hold floodwater. In communities experiencing extreme heat, updating paving materials on roads and creating more green space can help lower the temperature. In fire-prone areas, building more watchtowers helps detect wildfires early, saving lives. The administration is trying to block states from making polluters contribute to these efforts. The DOJ has also sued to stop state and local governments, like Hawai’i, from suing oil companies in state courts. It has even intervened on behalf of polluters in Suncor v. Boulder. Outside the courtroom, gas prices are soaring while oil and gas companies post record-breaking profits in the tens of billions of dollars. But the Trump administration is paying billions of your dollars to cancel affordable clean energy projects. Those taxpayer dollars go straight to energy companies. In Congress, oil-backed Republicans introduced the so-called “Stop Climate Shakedowns Act.” The bill would give fossil fuel companies blanket immunity from state superfund laws and climate lawsuits filed in any court. That’s the same special treatment that Republicans on the Supreme Court are about to consider. The bill’s sponsors have deep ties to the oil industry. Senator Ted Cruz (R-TX) has long been a darling of the oil and gas industry. In 2024, he raised $1.4 million in campaign contributions from the fossil fuel industry. The oil and gas industry has given Rep. Harriet Hageman’s (R-WY) campaign hundreds of thousands of dollars. The president and the Congress should be trying to protect regular people, not just the Big Polluters. And they should be trying to reform a Supreme Court that has been corrupted by the Big Polluters. Unfortunately, right now they’re not doing either. Again and again, Big Oil has lied and cheated to protect its profits. But everyday people have a right to make corporations pay for the destruction they cause. Our Congress, our judges, and our president should protect the people, not polluters’ profits. Join LCV and tell your members of Congress: stop letting Big Oil off the hook! Make sure our judges work for the people and the law, not Big Polluters and their political allies. Again and again, Big Oil has lied and cheated to protect its profits. title: Doe v. State of Kansas - American Civil Liberties Union
content: Two transgender residents of Kansas filed a lawsuit in state court challenging SB 244, a state law enacted in 2026 that immediately invalidated the driver’s licenses of transgender people across the state and which authorizes anyone to sue anybody they suspect of being transgender for using the “wrong” restroom in government buildings. By completing this form, I agree to receive occasional emails per the terms of the ACLU's privacy statement. In early 2026, the Kansas state legislature passed SB 244, a law which prohibits transgender people from using public restrooms on government property that align with their gender identity and establishes a private right of action that allows anyone who suspects someone is transgender and in violation of the law to sue that person for “damages” totaling $1,000. The law also invalidates state-issued driver’s licenses with updated gender markers that reflect the carrier’s gender identity. In February 2026, transgender people across the state received letters from the state Department of Revenue’s Division of Vehicles informing them that their driver’s licenses “will no longer be valid,” effective immediately. SB 244 also prohibits transgender Kansans – or those born in Kansas - from updating the gender marker on state-issued birth certificates and driver’s licenses in the future. The same day SB 244 went into effect, the American Civil Liberties Union, the ACLU of Kansas, and Ballard Spahr LLP filed a lawsuit challenging SB 244 in the District Court of Douglas County on behalf of two transgender men who had their driver’s licenses invalidated under the law. The lawsuit charges that SB 244 violates the Kansas Constitution’s protections for personal autonomy, privacy, equality under the law, due process, and freedom of speech. “The invalidation of state-issued IDs threatens to out transgender people against their will every time they apply for a job, rent an apartment, or interact with police,” said Harper Seldin, Senior Staff Attorney for the ACLU’s LGBTQ & HIV Rights Project. “Taken as a whole, SB 244 is a transparent attempt to deny transgender people autonomy over their own identities and push them out of public life altogether.” Click here to learn more about SB 244 and what it means for transgender people. If you or a loved one is impacted by Senate Bill 244 becoming a law, contact us by visiting aclu.org/KS_SB244. We want to hear from you. Update: A hearing on the motion for a preliminary injunction blocking enforcement of SB 244 has been scheduled for September 29, 2026. Kansas State Court Denies Temporary Restraining Order Against State Law Invalidating IDs and Restricting Bathroom Access for Transgender People Transgender Kansans Challenge State Law Invalidating Their Driver’s Licenses and Allowing Them to Be Sued for Using Public Restrooms
